# Hosea 1: research notes

**What I couldn't find:** I had a limited number of searches and page reads, so some sources are missing. There's nothing here from Methodist or Wesleyan sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Orthodox sites (oca.org), bibleodyssey.org or the NET Bible notes. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Where a teacher's church tradition is named below, the source page itself says so or it is clear from the teacher's name (Calvin). Otherwise I've left the tradition unlabelled.

---

**v. 1**
- **The name and the setting.** Hosea's name means "salvation" and comes from the same Hebrew root as *Joshua* and *Jesus*. His work was in the northern kingdom. He calls Israel's king "our king" (7:5). He lists the kings of Judah so that readers in Judah would have a reference point. He began under Jeroboam II, a time of wealth but spiritual decay. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-1/
- **Dates.** Tully (Gospel Coalition) dates Hosea to about 755–725 BC. The superscription "identifies the book's author and the date of his ministry." He also says Hosea is the only writing prophet who was a native of the northern kingdom. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/hosea/
- **"Through Hosea."** Coffman prefers "through Hosea" to "unto Hosea": the message is God's word, not just the prophet's. He thinks Judah's kings are listed because the prophets saw that God's true seat was in Jerusalem, not Samaria. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/hosea-1.html

**v. 2: the big debate (was the marriage real?)**
- **Why the command.** It is a prophetic "sign-act." The Hebrew word (*zanah*) means illicit sexual activity. The text does not technically call her a "prostitute" but rather describes the actions which characterize her. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/hosea/
- **Feeling what God feels.** Guzik says the command puts Hosea where he feels what God feels when His people turn to idols. Whether Gomer was already a prostitute or became one later may be the case, but we don't know this from the text. It could go either way. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/hosea/hosea-1.cfm
- **Four older positions.** Bob Utley (bible.org) lists them: Origen said that nothing unworthy of God should be taken literally, but must be spiritualized /allegorized; Jerome and Iben Ezra (many rabbis) interpret this as a vision; Calvin and E. J. Young interpret this as an allegory; and Martin Luther interprets this as Gomer being a faithful wife and they only acted out this drama to convey the message. https://bible.org/seriespage/hosea-1
- **Gill: a parable.** Gill says a literal marriage to a harlot would look like approving of sin. It seems best therefore to understand the whole as a parable. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/msg/hosea/1-2.html
- **Coffman: real, and Gomer was innocent at first.** He treats the marriage as historical. Because Israel *fell away* from God, Gomer must have been innocent at the start. He also notes that only priests were forbidden to marry a harlot. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/hosea-1.html
- **Boice, quoted by Guzik, against reading it as fiction:** "If Hosea's story cannot be real (because 'God could not ask a man to marry an unfaithful woman'), then neither is the story of salvation real, because that is precisely what Christ has done for us." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-1/
- **Looking back.** An older commentary on Bible Hub (not named on the page) suggests Hosea discovered her wickedness only after the marriage. Looking back later, he saw it as a picture of the nation's wrong against God. https://biblehub.com/hosea/1-2.htm
- **Catholic view.** The old Catholic Encyclopedia says the hypothesis most in favor at present says that the marriage is historical. It also admits it is hard to believe God would order a prophet to marry a wife so that she would be unfaithful. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/osee
- **Douay-Rheims note (Catholic).** "Wife of fornications" means a woman who had been given to fornication. This pictured Israel's spiritual fornication. https://www.ccel.org/c/challoner/douayrheims/Osee/01.html

**v. 3**
- **Gomer's name.** Coffman notes that "Diblaim" has been read as "fig-cakes." Some take that as a sign she was a Baal prostitute, but he says this is by no means certain. He argues that "bore *him* a son" shows the first child was Hosea's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/hosea-1.html
- **The names are real names.** The Catholic Encyclopedia supports a historical marriage partly because "Gomer" and "Debelaim" carry no symbolic meaning. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/osee
- **Obedience.** Hosea showed real obedience. Guzik thinks Gomer kept on in prostitution after the marriage. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-1/

**v. 4: why punish Jehu when God approved him (2 Kings 10:30)?**
- **Calvin (Reformed).** Jehu was God's instrument but did not act for God. That slaughter with regard to Jehu was robbery; with regard to God it was a just revenge. Jehu then kept up the old false worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/1-4.html
- **Barnes:** if we do what is the will of God for any end of our own, for anything except God, we do, in fact, our own will, not God's. Matthew Henry makes the same point: the act was right but done in the wrong spirit, for Jehu's own advancement. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/1-4.html
- **Constable.** Jehu also killed King Ahaziah of Judah and 42 relatives, which went beyond God's command. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/1-4.html
- **Ligonier:** the Lord never told Jehu to destroy the family and friends of Judah's king. Jehu took things too far. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jehu-destroys-ahabs-line
- **Kaiser (via Precept Austin).** Being God's chosen tool to punish is one thing. It doesn't mean God approves the *way* the job was done. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-9-commentary
- **The name "Jezreel."** It means "God sows." Guzik also gives "scattered." He notes the fulfilment: Jehu's line ended when Zechariah was killed after six months (2 Kings 15:8–10). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-1/ ; https://biblehub.com/hosea/1-4.htm

**v. 5**
- **The broken bow.** Guzik quotes Hubbard: the bow stood for military power, so a broken bow means loss of power. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-1/
- **Fulfilment.** Coffman sees this fulfilled in Shalmaneser's defeat of Israel in that valley. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/hosea-1.html

**v. 6**
- **"No Mercy."** Lo-ruhamah means "No Mercy." Each time the child was called, people were reminded of the coming judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-1/
- **Who was the father?** Coffman points out that the text does *not* say Gomer bore this child "to him." That raises the question of who the father was. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/hosea-1.html
- Another writer on Precept Austin makes the same point. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea_devotionals

**v. 7**
- **How it was fulfilled.** Guzik ties this to the angel striking down 185,000 Assyrians (2 Kings 19:35). He adds that mercy is never deserved, so God may show mercy to whom He will (Romans 9:15). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-1/
- **Only a delay.** Coffman calls Judah's rescue only a temporary reprieve. Judah later went into exile in Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/hosea-1.html

**vv. 8–9**
- **Lo-ammi.** Guzik suggests this son may really not have been Hosea's. He reads "not My people" as God stating a fact the people had already chosen, more than as a penalty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-1/
- **"I am not your I AM."** Coffman quotes Mays: the Hebrew echoes the divine name of Exodus 3:14, as if God says "I am not your I-AM." It declares the covenant no longer in force. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/hosea-1.html
- **Fast pregnancies.** Utley says the quick births may reflect Gomer's ongoing sexual activity. https://bible.org/seriespage/hosea-1

**v. 10: a real disagreement (Israel, the church, or both?)**
- **Coffman: the Gentiles only.** He calls the verse a definite prophecy of Gentiles coming in, based on Romans 9:25–26. He insists This is a definite promise and prophecy of the coming of the Gentiles into the favor of God. Elsewhere he says there are no Bible promises of restoring physical Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/hosea-1.html
- **Both now and later.** One commentary on Bible Hub reads it spiritually, as believing Jews and Gentiles, but says it is To be fulfilled in its literal fulness hereafter in Israel's restoration (Ro 11:26). Barnes sees two future stages, with the place of rejection becoming the place of restoration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/1-10.htm
- **Paul's use of the verse.** The Expositor's Greek Testament says Paul applies to Gentiles words that first spoke of Israel's restoration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/9-25.htm
- **Light of Israel commentary.** It says Paul uses this verse to explain how believing Gentiles are now part of Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/1-10.html
- **"The living God."** The phrase is set against Baal and lifeless idols. https://biblehub.com/hosea/1-10.htm

**v. 11**
- **Trapp: the head is Christ.** He identifies the "one head" as Christ, "David their King" (3:5). He also argues against the Roman Catholic claim that Peter (Cephas) is the head: Judah and Israel shall appoint to themselves one head, not more than one. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/hos-1.cfm
- **Calvin.** Wherever God speaks of restoration, He points the faithful to David as their one king. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/1-11.html
- **Coffman: fulfilled at Pentecost.** He sees it fulfilled at Pentecost, with Christ as the head. The return from Babylon was too small to fit the prophecy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/1-11.html
- **Houbigant: still future for the Jews.** Quoted on Bible Hub, he takes the promise to concern the Jews' final condition under the Messiah. Barnes adds that both Judah and Israel are gathered into the one church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/1-11.htm
- **Catholic chapter heading.** The Douay-Rheims summary of the chapter says it foretells their redemption by Christ. https://www.ccel.org/c/challoner/douayrheims/Osee/01.html
